final.title: Why proof-of-concept debt survives
final.body:
Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved part of the problem, but nobody made it part of daily work. In a small business, that often looks like a manual workflow for customer questions, invoice data, lead routing, or data sync that keeps getting patched with a demo instead of a decision.

The useful question is not “should we use AI everywhere?” It is: once this workflow is automated, who owns running it day to day, and do they have time to do that job? If the answer is unclear, the pilot tends to become shelf-ware. Not because the model is bad, but because the operating decision was never made.

That is the bounded decision Bareni is built around. The diagnostic looks at one recurring workflow, checks honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, defines scope, fixed price, and measures. Finished code and the relevant accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start; retainer support is optional. Timings are intended scope, not a promise.

So the next step is simple: pick one repeatable workflow you touch every week and write down the owner before you build anything. If you cannot name that person, clarify that first. The pilot that ships and stays integrated is the one with an owner.

Proof-of-concept debt usually survives for one boring reason: the pilot solved part of the problem, but nobody made it part of daily work. For an owner-operator, that often looks like a manual workflow that keeps getting repeated while a clever demo sits on the side.
